Warfe Tupas Engracia widely known as "The Singing Octogenarian Doctor," is a Filipino physician, poet, and cultural historian. A Fellow of the Philippine College of Radiology and Knight Grand Cross of Rizal (Fifth Degree), Engracia is also an accomplished musician, poet, and advocate for the preservation of the Malay heritage. His multifaceted achievements have earned him numerous accolades and recognition both nationally and internationally.
Early life and education
Early Life and Ancestry
Warfe Tupas Engracia was born into a family with deep cultural ties to Cebu, Philippines. He traces his lineage to Rajah Tupas, the last Malay king of Cebu. His early fascination with history, poetry, and the cultural identity of the Malay people inspired many of his life's endeavors. His parents, Soledad Barrera Tupas and Felipe Tambasal (Ozal) Engracia, played pivotal roles in shaping his passion for heritage and the arts.
Medical career
Engracia earned his medical degree and became a respected radiologist. He established King Tupas Medical Services in 1997 and launched a mobile medical van service in 2001, both named after his ancestral figure Rajah Tupas. His commitment to public health is paralleled by his efforts to uplift Filipino and Malay culture through education and the arts.
Literary and Musical Contributions
Dr. Engracia is renowned for his literary works, including the acclaimed poem Aku ang Tuud ("I Am The Stump"). This poem, which symbolizes resilience and cultural revival, received a standing ovation at the 2001 World Conference of Malay People held at the World Trade Center in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. His body of work spans poetry, historical essays, and musical compositions, all of which emphasize the unity and shared heritage of the Malay race.
Philosophy and Cultural Advocacy
He has also worked as a consultant with the Engracia's writings reflect his deep commitment to preserving the Malay cultural identity. He has spoken extensively about the importance of embracing and understanding the shared history of Southeast Asian nations. His advocacy efforts have led to increased recognition of the contributions of historical figures such as Dr. José Rizal and Apolinario Mabini in promoting Malay unity and self-determination.
Awards and Honors
Fellow of the Philippine College of Radiology
Knight Grand Cross of Rizal (Fifth Degree)
Doctor of Humanities (Honoris Causa, NCU, USA)
Doctor of Philosophy (PhD TL)
Personal Life
Warfe Tupas Engracia is the father of several children, including Christine Grace (deceased), Mariquit Socoro, Ellen Grace, Jasmin, Ken Mark, Athena Ever, and Christopher Joshua. He continues to inspire his community through his artistic, medical, and cultural endeavors.
Social media presence
Engracia started maintaining an online presence when he set up a YouTube channel in 2014, where he posts videos providing health tips and medical explainers targeted to a general audience.[8] As of February 2025, his YouTube channel "Dr.Warfe-Operation Tabang /HELP" has 275 subscribers, and a total viewcount of 35,477 times.
Legacy
Often described as a modern-day Renaissance figure, Dr. Warfe Tupas Engracia remains a significant advocate for cultural unity and heritage in the Philippines and across the Malay world. His work continues to influence both academic and cultural institutions, with a lasting impact on the preservation of Southeast Asian identity.
